analysis.one_liner: Tightens import rules, labeling, and funding conditions on palm oil tied to deforestation and labor abuses.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to five House committees in November 2021 and never received a markup or floor vote before the Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would cover imported palm oil under a law against trafficking in illegally taken wildlife and plants, require foods to clearly label palm oil ingredients and their country of origin, block imported palm oil from counting as renewable fuel, and bar federal funds from supporting palm oil cultivation abroad unless it meets sustainability and human-rights standards. It never got a committee vote or a floor vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Shoppers get clearer labels showing palm oil content and country of origin. Forested land, wildlife habitats, and communities near palm oil plantations abroad gain protection, since federal money and development loans could not fund cultivation that causes deforestation, forced labor, or human trafficking unless certified sustainable. Workers on palm oil plantations gain from conditions requiring certification standards that prioritize their human rights.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Consumers, forests, and plantation workers abroad

how_it_helps.text: Removes palm oil from an existing exemption for 'common cultivars and common food crops,' bringing imported palm oil within the Lacey Act's import declaration and enforcement requirements [S3].
Requires foods containing imported palm oil ingredients to list them by common or usual name with all components, and adds palm oil to country-of-origin labeling requirements [S3].

Bars federal funds from supporting palm oil cultivation or processing abroad unless the Secretary of State certifies it will not cause deforestation, water contamination, forced displacement, human trafficking, forced or child labor, or wildlife trafficking [S3].
Prohibits imported palm oil products from being treated as renewable fuel under the Clean Air Act's renewable fuel program, except as the EPA Administrator allows [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Importers of palm oil and food manufacturers using it would bear new compliance costs: Lacey Act import declarations unless they obtain certification, ingredient and country-of-origin labeling, and the loss of any renewable-fuel credit value. Palm oil growers in producing countries such as Indonesia and Malaysia would face pressure to obtain sustainability certification to keep access to the U.S. market.
analysis.who_pays_short: Palm oil importers and food manufacturers

drawbacks.text: The bill creates a certification shortcut: palm oil meeting an approved nongovernmental sustainability standard would not need a Lacey Act import declaration, and the documentation would count as 'due care,' which could shield importers of improperly certified products from liability [S3].

It singles out one commodity for stricter import rules and labeling, adding compliance costs for food and consumer-goods manufacturers and creating potential trade friction with palm oil-exporting countries [S3].
Excluding palm oil from the renewable fuel program removes one feedstock option from biofuel producers [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The consumer protections and environmental and labor safeguards are real but targeted at one commodity, and the compliance costs fall on importers and food makers rather than being spread broadly. The main design weakness is the certification shortcut, which relies on private standards (the bill specifically considers the Roundtable for Sustainable Palm Oil's standard) to substitute for government import declarations, a pathway that could be leniently administered. On balance the bill's benefits to consumers and to communities and forests abroad outweigh its modest economic costs, though its single sponsor and single cosponsor made its prospects poor from the start.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to five House committees, then to three subcommittees, and none of them acted on it before the 117th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. John Garamendi introduced the bill on November 4, 2021, with introductory remarks in the Congressional Record [S1] [S5].
It was referred to the Committees on Agriculture, Energy and Commerce, Foreign Affairs, Financial Services, and Natural Resources [S1] [S5].
Within its first month it was further referred to the subcommittees on Health, Water Oceans and Wildlife, and Livestock and Foreign Agriculture [S5].
The bill attracted one cosponsor, a House Democrat [S4].
No committee held a markup, no subcommittee or committee reported it, and the House never voted on it before the Congress ended on January 3, 2023 [S1] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Palm oil importers, food manufacturers using palm oil, and uncertified growers abroad are better off because nothing changed: no new import declarations, labeling rules, or funding conditions took effect. Consumers and communities abroad remain without the protections the bill offered.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Palm oil importers and food makers

for.name: Rep. John Garamendi
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on it [S1] [S5].

sides.party_line_note: No opposition ever appears on the record; the bill drew one cosponsor from the sponsor's own party and simply died in committee without a vote.

industries.note: The bill subjects imported palm oil to Lacey Act declarations and enforcement and to labeling rules, raising costs for the trade; but importers meeting an approved sustainability certification get a streamlined entry path without an import declaration. Growers that stay uncertified lose U.S. market advantages, and their interest in avoiding these rules runs against the protections consumers and forest communities would gain.

industries.industry: Sustainable palm oil certification bodies (including the Roundtable for Sustainable Palm Oil)
industries.note: The bill makes private nongovernmental certification the official channel: certified palm oil skips Lacey Act declarations and certification becomes the condition for federal funding of cultivation abroad. That locks in the certifiers' gatekeeping role over a public good, though their standards are supposed to prioritize deforestation prevention and worker and community rights.

industries.industry: Food and consumer-goods manufacturers using palm oil
industries.note: They would bear new costs to label palm oil ingredients in detail and list country of origin, plus documentation requirements at the port of entry. The industry's interest in minimizing disclosure runs against shoppers' ability to know what is in their food and where it came from.
Imported palm oil would be barred from counting toward renewable fuel requirements, removing a cheap feedstock pathway the industry could otherwise use.
